sections.overview: The moose is the largest living deer, inhabiting northern forests of North America and Eurasia, from Alaska and Canada to Scandinavia, Russia, northern China and Mongolia. In British English it is often called elk.
sections.identification: A shoulder hump, heavy body, long legs and drooping muzzle define its shape. Only males grow annual antlers: broad palms are common in North America, narrower forms occur in Eurasia. Coat colour ranges from brown to nearly black. Long legs cross deep snow; nostrils close underwater, aiding submerged feeding. Adults typically stand about 1.5–2.1 m at the shoulder. British Columbia reports average masses of about 450–500 kg for males and 340–420 kg for females; very large males can reach about 680 kg. The antlers of males can span about 1.5 m, but antler width varies and is not body width.
sections.habitat: Moose favour northern woodland, young forest, wetlands and shores. In Alaska they use river corridors, timberline plateaus and burns where willow, birch and aspen regrow. Lakes and marshes offer food and cover. Seasonal movements link feeding, calving, rutting and wintering areas.
sections.diet: Food varies with season and supply. In summer it eats leaves, herbs and shallow-water plants; spring also brings grazing. Woody shoots, especially willow, birch and aspen, matter more in autumn and winter. Its long muzzle and closable nostrils help crop submerged plants.
sections.behavior: Moose are usually solitary; cows stay with calves, and adults meet more during the autumn rut. Males push antlers against rivals; winners may mate with several females. Seasonal movements vary locally. Daily activity centres on feeding, resting and rumination.
sections.reproduction: In Alaska, mating peaks in late September and early October. After about 230 days, females calve in spring, usually producing one calf; twins occur in favourable conditions. Calves grow quickly, nurse through summer and are usually weaned in autumn, remaining with their mother into the next year.
sections.ecology: Browsing shrubs, saplings and aquatic plants affects forest regeneration. At unusually high density in Forillon, Parks Canada documents major vegetation changes. That local case shows how abundant moose can shape plant communities; effects vary with population and habitat.
sections.conservation: The global IUCN assessment (last assessed 27 September 2015; published 2016) classed moose as Least Concern, with an increasing overall trend. It cited habitat alteration as a major human threat. This dated assessment is not a current survey of regional populations.
